title: Temperature and its Measurement
intro: When you say 'hot tea' or 'cold water', you're describing temperature. This chapter teaches you what temperature really is, how a thermometer measures it, and why measuring temperature carefully matters at home and in hospitals.

sections.heading: Hot, Cold, and Why Touch Isn't Enough
bullets: We feel hotness or coldness whenever we touch something — soup is hot, ice is cold.
Different people may feel the same water as warm or cold, depending on what they touched before.
Try this: put one hand in warm water and one in cold for a minute, then put both in a bowl of room-temperature water. Each hand feels something different!
Because touch can mislead, we use an instrument to measure exactly how hot or cold something is.

sections.heading: What Is Temperature?
bullets: Temperature is a number that tells us how hot or cold an object is.
Higher numbers mean hotter; lower numbers mean colder.
The most common unit used worldwide is the degree Celsius (°C).
On the Celsius scale, water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at sea level.
Normal human body temperature is about 37 °C; room temperature is around 25 °C.

sections.heading: Thermometers
bullets: A thermometer is the instrument we use to measure temperature.
Old liquid-in-glass thermometers contain coloured alcohol or mercury inside a thin glass tube.
When the bulb gets hotter, the liquid expands and rises in the tube; when it cools, the liquid drops.
Digital thermometers show the reading directly on a screen and give a beep when ready.
Clinical thermometers are special: they have a smaller range (35 °C to 42 °C) suitable for body temperature.

sections.heading: Reading a Thermometer Carefully
bullets: Hold the thermometer straight, with the bulb in the substance whose temperature you want.
Wait until the liquid stops moving, then read the level at eye level so you don't get a parallax error.
Note the value with units, e.g., 32 °C, not just 32.
Before using a clinical thermometer, give it a few quick downward shakes so the mercury starts low.
Wash the thermometer with cool water and antiseptic before and after each use, and never put it in boiling water.

sections.heading: Body Temperature and Health
bullets: Normal body temperature is about 37 °C, though it can vary slightly across the day.
If body temperature rises above 37.5 °C, the person likely has a fever.
When you have an infection, the body raises its temperature to fight germs.
Very low body temperature is also dangerous — it can happen in extreme cold.
Doctors and nurses use thermometers many times a day to check patients.

sections.heading: Temperature in Daily Life
bullets: Cookbooks tell you to pre-heat the oven to a temperature like 180 °C; ovens have thermometers built in.
Refrigerators keep food at low temperature so germs grow slowly.
Air conditioners and heaters change room temperature to make us comfortable.
Weather reports give the day's high and low temperature; this helps us decide what to wear.
Vaccines must be stored in cold boxes — temperature-sensitive medicines lose effect if they get too warm.

key_takeaways: Temperature is the measured hotness or coldness of an object.
Touch can mislead, so we use a thermometer for accurate measurement.
We use the Celsius scale: water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.
Clinical thermometers measure body temperature (range 35–42 °C); normal is about 37 °C.
Read at eye level, wait for the reading to settle, and clean the thermometer before and after.
Temperature matters in cooking, health, weather, and storage of food and medicines.

glossary.definition: A measure of how hot or cold an object is, given as a number with units.
An instrument used to measure temperature.
The unit of temperature used worldwide; water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.
A thermometer with a small range, used to measure human body temperature.
A silvery liquid metal once used inside thermometers; now mostly replaced by alcohol or digital sensors.
A body temperature above the normal of about 37 °C, usually a sign of infection.
An error that comes from reading a scale from the side instead of straight on.
To clean an instrument with antiseptic so it does not spread germs.
